entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams is once again the talk of the NFL, but he's controlling the conversation now
entries.summary: <p>In the roaring sea of fans at Lumen Field on Monday night before <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>’ game against the Seahawks, quarterback Caleb Williams focused in on a single speck in the crowd.</p><p>As he huddled briefly with teammates during pre-game warmups, he saw a Seattle fan staring directly at him with a white posterboard with black letters written in marker that read, “CALEB WILLIAMS FAKES INJURIES – PAINTS HIS NAILS PINK.” It stuck with Williams well after he carved up the Seahawks for the Bears’ most impressive win of his career, and he posted it on Instagram.</p><p>Even as Williams is riding higher than ever and has been the talk of every NFL show this week, he’s still searching for fuel.</p><p>“Those are fun,” he said Wednesday. “Sometimes when you go into games, you just need one thing. That was maybe it.”</p><p>Turns out making a nasty sign for Williams is counterproductive. He’s unfazed by the whiplash of his popularity, seeming to find usefulness in best and worst of it.</p><p>He brimmed with confidence going into the season after taking the cover of the new Madden game, then burned inside when a wave of mockery crashed on him after hurting his hamstring in Week 2 and leaving the field in tears. The positive and negative drive him equally.</p><p>He’s at a new high point now, though, after surging into the MVP race. He’s been hot the last three games, looking like a championship-level quarterback, and — like all things with Williams — the nation has noticed.</p><p>The lasting memory from Seattle wasn’t what he did on the field, though he was sharp in completing 24 of 34 passes for 247 yards and a touchdown for a 101.0 passer rating. Instead, it was his post-game appearance on SportsCenter with Scott Van Pelt.</p><p>With a throng of Bears fans sticking around to watch, Williams could barely talk over the constant chant of “M-V-P,” which predictably veered off into “Green Bay sucks” and various screams of, “We love you,” while he tried to answer Van Pelt’s questions.</p><p>That was only the beginning this week. Williams has always been front and center locally, but since Monday it’s been impossible to turn on any sports show on TV and avoid his face.</p><p>It’s no wonder that NBC opted to hold on to the Bears’ upcoming home game against the Buccaneers for “Sunday Night Football” rather than flex it out, even as the Bucs are 3-5 and irrelevant.</p><p>Anything with Williams is relevant. You bring the cameras, he’ll bring the star power. America will be glued to the game just to see him.</p><p>That’s what the Bears always hoped would happen when they drafted him No. 1 overall in 2024. They believed they were getting a quarterback who not only had the talent to bury their woeful history at the position, but be the face of the team as a new Chicago sports icon and lead them out of obscurity.</p><p>It took time, more than the Bears initially thought, and the volatility of Williams’ fame tracked with his performance. He lost the spotlight after the draft when No. 2 pick Jayden Daniels raced ahead of him, then he reasserted himself with an artful display in London to beat the Jaguars. Then the season fell apart, and Williams <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >was back to seeing his body language and facial expressions under a microscope</a>.</p><p>It took a while last season, too, as coach Ben Johnson drove him so hard that Williams later playfully described the early part of their relationship as fragile. Williams made amazing plays, many with the game on the line, but struggled in the basics — a combination that made him perfect debate material for talk shows.</p><p>“People are going to say what they have to say; I can’t please everybody,” Williams said. “That’s not my job. My job is to go win."</p><p>The last three weeks, though, he has taken control of the conversation.</p><p>Williams is fifth in the NFL in passer rating (104.6), second in completion percentage (70.9) and 11th in yards per game (253.4) — all of which are a leap from where he was last season.</p><p>There is no other side of the argument when he’s playing like this. Even those who dislike him for superficial reasons must concede he’s turning into an elite quarterback.</p><p>“If you like it or don’t like it,” he said, “you’ve got to deal with it.”</p><p>The improvement has pushed him to the peak of his popularity thus far, but it’s still rising.</p>

entries.title: Bears coach Ben Johnson has mastered the art of turning the page
entries.summary: <p>If all things were equal, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ first team meeting of each week would feel the same after a win as it did after a loss. Corrections would be made with impersonal precision.</p><p>That’s not the case, though, inside Halas Hall or anywhere else.</p><p>But Ben Johnson can try.</p><p>“We try to be as consistent as we possibly can and we tell them the truth and it's not about hurting feelings or anything like that,” the Bears coach said Wednesday. “We're all in the business of getting better.”</p><p>That’s as true now — in a week the football-loving world officially fell in love with the Bears after a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/02/bears-seahawks-score-13-9-halftime-monday-night-football-caleb-williams-ben-johnson-physicality-nfl" >34-17 win in Seattle </a>— as it’s been at any point in Johnson’s career. And that's why, even in the minutes after beating the defending Super Bowl champions Monday night, Bears players were hesitant to make any grand declarations about the message they sent to the league.</p><p>“We’re not really focused on everybody else … ” safety Cam Lewis said. “It was just our next game.”</p><p>Said receiver Kalif Raymond: “We’ve still got a lot of season left.”</p><p>And defensive end Montez Sweat: “The tape speaks for itself.”</p><p>They’re channeling a head coach that, in his Bears career, has mastered the art of turning the page — especially after victories. He’s had a lot more experience dealing with wins than losses, too. Johnson has won 68% of his regular season games in a year-and-a-half, the highest percentage by any Bears head coach since George Halas retired in 1967. Amazingly, a win Sunday would push him past Halas and behind only Ralph Jones, who last coached for the Bears in 1932, in franchise annals.</p><p>Johnson hasn’t won this many games without knowing how to get his players to turn the page from week-to-week. He can’t tell his players to ignore the outside world — “We’re in a day and age where everybody sees everything on their cell phones,” he said — but he can encourage them to put zero stock in it.</p><p>“We’ve gotta keep winning,” Johnson said. “We’ve gotta win each and every week. We gotta go 1-0 this week. That’s all we care about. That’s all we’ve talked about for the last year and a half in this building, and that doesn’t change, no matter what our record is and what’s happened previously. We’re gonna go right back to work. We’re gonna prepare just like we’ve been doing.”</p><p>That’s in part how the Bears won four consecutive games last year and then, after a loss, five more in a row. The Bears currently are riding a three-game winning streak, their third stretch with at least that many wins since Johnson’s arrival. Coach Matt Eberflus, by contrast, had one three-game winning streak in almost three seasons.</p><p>Johnson's turn-the-page mantra is not just messaging, either. It’s starts with film study.</p><p>“I believe in the coaching staff, I believe in the players, I believe in our process,” Johnson said. “And our process is one of hard work and belief. That’s what we just continue to hone into.”</p><p>Players naturally take coaching points with a better attitude after wins. It’s human nature.</p><p>But that doesn’t make the corrections any less important.</p><p>“When you win, all the mistakes are minimized,” Johnson said. “And then when you lose, everything gets magnified to the nth degree. But they're still there. Each and every game, there's always things that we've got to clean up and get better at.”</p><p>If anything, Johnson said, he can coach his players harder after wins that he can after losses.</p><p>“And yet, at the same time,” he said, “we try to be as consistent as we possibly can be throughout.”<br></p>

entries.title: Blue wave comes ashore in red Indiana
entries.summary: <p>The blue wave that struck Tuesday night nationwide also hit in parts of normally red Indiana.</p><p>Democrats picked up an additional Congressional seat and won the party's first statewide race in 14 years, when Beau Bayh won the race for Indiana secretary of state.</p><p>U.S. Rep. Frank J. Mrvan won re-election Tuesday night and his 4th overall term to Washington to represent Northwest Indiana, a historically blue district.</p><p>Mrvan beat out Republican challenger Barb Regnitz in a traditionally Democrat-leaning district targeted last year by President Trump. As in other states, Trump had pushed state lawmakers to draw new congressional district lines that would help Republicans gain seats in Congress, but the General Assembly voted that down.</p><p>“I'm connected to the district. I believe that fighting for lower fuel costs when it comes to gasoline and diesel. Voting for the War Powers Act to make sure the (Trump) administration has a strategy was something that was a difference maker,” Mrvan said Wednesday. “We spent a lot of time knocking on doors, in union halls talking to union members. I just think we were able to connect and I understand that our district wants results. We have a lot of hard work ahead of us.”</p><p>One of the first things Mrvan wants to tackle once the Democratic majority is sworn in next year is reducing fuel costs for families and farmers.</p><p>“The farmers are getting crushed by the diesel costs for their combines and to move goods, which means our grocery costs are going to go up,” Mrvan said. “We've got to get a handle on our costs, and we've got to end — and have a strategic plan to end — the war in Iran.”</p><p>A member of the House Appropriations Committee, Mrvan pushed for the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to investigate NIPSCO due to the power outages that occurred after a storm hit Northwest Indiana in August. The storm knocked out power to thousands of residents, and power to some areas, including many in Gary, was not restored for weeks. </p><p>As a member of the committee, Mrvan helps set the budget for the Federal Emergency Management Agency. Following the storm, President Trump declared Indiana a federal disaster area, which provided emergency funding to some residents.</p><p>Mrvan will join two fellow Democrats in Congress; incumbent Rep. Andre Carson won re-election to his 7th District seat in Indianapolis and J.D. Ford won an unexpected victory over incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Victoria Spartz in the 5th District, which includes the suburbs north of Indianapolis, once a reliably Republican area.</p><p>In that secretary of state's race, Bayh beat Republican Max Engling, 51.8% to 42.6%, with about 98% of the vote counted. </p><p>Bayh became the first Democrat to win a statewide office since 2012, and his victory came 40 years after his father, Evan Bayh, won that same office. Evan Bayh went on to serve as governor and in the U.S. Senate. Beau Bayh is continuing a political lineage that started with his grandfather, the late U.S. Sen. Birch Bayh.</p><p>Hoosier Democrats even broke the Indiana GOP’s 20-year supermajority in the General Assembly, flipping 10 seats in the Indiana House and picking up four seats in the Indiana Senate, which could make things a little more difficult for Republican Gov. Mike Braun.</p><p>“You elected over a dozen new Democratic legislators who are ready to hold Mike Braun’s administration accountable on day one. In January there will be more Hoosier Democrats serving in the state legislature than in decades," said Indiana Democratic Party chair Karen Tallian.</p><p>Tallian also touted Mrvan’s victory.</p><p>“No one works harder for the people of Northwest Indiana than Congressman Frank Mrvan. The reason Region voters keep sending him back to Congress with larger and larger margins is because they know he goes to work everyday to make life more affordable, stand up for the rights of working people, and ensure Northwest Indiana gets a fair shake,” Tallian said in a written statement.</p><p><i>Michael Puente is a reporter and weekend anchor for WBEZ. Reach him at </i><a class="Link" href="mailto:mpuente@wbez.org" target="_blank" ><i><u>mpuente@wbez.org</u></i></a><i>.</i></p>

entries.title: Bulls rookie Dailyn Swain headed to G League to get some playing time
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK — Dailyn Swain would jump into a pickup game at DePaul’s Ray Meyer Rec Center right about now if it meant him getting some run.</p><p>That’s where the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> rookie is these days, sitting, waiting and chomping at the bit to get back to competing.</p><p>Now he’ll get his chance.</p><p>Coach Tiago Splitter revealed the plan for Swain on Wednesday, as the franchise will send him, Tobe Awaka and Jaylin Sellers out to the Windy City Bulls of the G League to get some minutes on Friday and Saturday. The baby Bulls host back-to-back games against the Noblesville Boom, while the big-boy squad has a break in the schedule until the Sunday afternoon game with the 76ers.</p><p>“I think Dailyn, Jaylin and Tobe, those are the guys that we want to focus on this month of November,” Splitter said. “Go and get minutes, get shots up. Repetition is going to be important for them.”</p><p>Not the only thing either.</p><p>“It’s an opportunity to get live reps,” Swain said of why he’s excited to head to Hoffman Estates for a few nights. “Obviously being out of the rotation up here, so I feel like it’s an opportunity to develop, work on the things, so that’s how I look at it.”</p><p>Swain, who was selected No. 15 overall in the June draft, wasn’t shy about listing what he needed to work on, either.</p><p>“All aspects of the game are obviously something you want to work on, but things that they’ve given me is the on-ball thing, definitely getting my shot off quicker, adjusting to the principles that we have, defending on-ball, defending a lot of elite guards, so working a variety of things,” he said.</p><p>Swain did get solid minutes in the preseason for the Bulls, again working on being a primary ball-handler, but had only appeared in one game since the regular season began and the wins and losses counted. And that one game was 12 minutes of mop-up duty against Boston in which Swain scored two points and had four turnovers.</p><p>He has been getting runs with teammates and the developmental staff, but competing against some different faces would be nice.</p><p>The good news is the plan is to also bring Swain back up when the Windy City Bulls are off, making sure he is still getting practice time with the varsity squad. That means more sitting, but not necessarily a bad thing for a 21-year-old rookie.</p><p>“It’s easy to make mental notes on that where it’s like, ‘OK, when I get my opportunity, that’s something I can’t do,’ “ Swain said. “If I see someone do something good it’s, ‘OK, take that and run with it.’ For me being young, I think it helps me.”</p><p></p><h3><b>Handling business</b></h3><h3></h3><p></p><p>Turnovers weren’t really an issue for Matas Buzelis in the first two years of his NBA career. Sure, there were hiccups now and then, but his ball-handling skills were always considered solid, especially for a 6-foot-8 forward.</p><p>Through the early days of this season, however, Buzelis was averaging a career-high three turnovers per game, including an ugly five-turnover showing in Philadelphia. He spent the last few days studying the film.</p><p>“Honestly sometimes I’m attacking and there’s no gap,” Buzelis said. “Last year, they wouldn’t even load to the ball, and I would just attack one-on-one, it was easy. I gotta find ways to attack offensively. I’m not even finding ways to attack. Just trying straight-line drive, but I’ll figure it out.”</p><p></p><h3><b>Nic of time</b></h3><h3></h3><p></p><p>Nic Claxton (hamstring) continued to ramp up activity but still wasn’t ready to make his Bulls debut Wednesday in New York.</p><p>There is still growing momentum he will play in his first game of the season on the three-game homestand.</p>

entries.title: Ravi Baichwal out at ABC 7 after station doesn't renew contract
entries.summary: <p>ABC 7 didn’t renew news anchor Ravi Baichwal’s contract, ending his 20-year run at the station.</p><p>“After 20 years with ABC 7, Ravi Baichwal has moved on following the conclusion of his contract,” an ABC 7/WLS-TV spokesperson said. “We wish him well in his next chapter.”</p><p>Baichwal, a Toronto native, had been anchoring the 5 and 6 p.m. newscasts since 2023 and won multiple Emmy Awards at ABC 7. In 2007, Baichwal was anchoring the 10 p.m. newscast from the station’s ground-level studio on State Street when <a class="Link" href="https://youtu.be/qPMUmoxNy2I?si=muvRgOpLFAPPCMzT" target="_blank" ><u>a minivan crashed into it</u></a>. Cameras captured his immediate reaction live.</p><p>Baichwal began his career in 1996 at the CBC and hosted his own morning show at CTV from 2002 to ’06.</p><p>In 2025, ABC 7 let go of investigative reporter Chuck Goudie, who’s now at NBC 5. In 2021, the station fired sports anchor Mark Giangreco after news anchor Cheryl Burton complained about a joke he made on the air.</p>

entries.title: Teen shot after fight in South Chicago
entries.summary: <p>A teen was shot after a fight in South Chicago escalated Wednesday afternoon, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The boy, 15, was in a physical altercation with an armed male, whose age wasn’t known, in the 8900 block of South Muskegon Avenue when he was shot at 1:43 p.m., police said. </p><p>The teen, wounded in his left thigh, was taken to Comer Children’s Hospital in good condition.</p><p>No one is in custody, police said. An investigation is ongoing.</p>

entries.title: Benet's Ed Stasys commits to Yale, continuing area's Ivy League pipeline
entries.summary: <p>With the recent commitment of Benet’s Ed Stasys to Yale, it’s another reminder of just how pivotally important recruiting the state of Illinois has become for Ivy League basketball programs.</p><p>While defections of high-level talent has led to Stasys becoming the state’s top-ranked prospect in the Class of 2027, this is still a monster commitment for the two-time defending Ivy League champs.</p><p>“The academic piece for my decision was definitely a factor, although I believe that Yale had some of the strongest basketball as well from the schools that I was considering,” Stasys said. “My family values academics. But that, along with basketball, were both even priorities.”</p><p>Stasys is just the next in line of top Illinois players who have opted for the combination of elite academics and Division I basketball. Buffalo Grove’s Alex Sirbu and Wheaton Academy’s Hayden Schroeder, both among the top 10 players in the senior class, are headed to Columbia and Penn, respectively.</p><p>This year’s current Ivy League freshman class has a whopping five Illinois products: New Trier’s Christopher Kirkpatrick at Princeton, DePaul Prep’s Rykan Woo at Brown, Deerfield’s Jake Pollack at Dartmouth, Loyola’s Trey Williams at Cornell and St. Ignatius’ Chris Bolte at Yale.</p><p>The impact in recent years is endless when it comes to local players propping up Ivy League basketball.</p><p>Glenbrook South’s Cooper Noard led the Ivy League in scoring last season in his final year at Cornell. New Trier’s Jake Fiegen was the conference’s third leading scorer.</p><p>Penn, the Ivy League’s NCAA Tournament qualifier, had four Illinois products on its roster, including leading scorer Ethan Roberts of Hersey and key contributors Dalton Scantlebury of Lane and AJ Levine of York.</p><p>John Poulakidas of Neuqua Valley was the Ivy’s leading scorer in 2023-24 while helping Yale to back-to-back NCAA Tournament appearances in 2024 and 2025.</p><p>Glenbard West’s Caden Pierce was the Ivy League Player of the Year in 2023-24.</p><p>The list goes on. New Trier’s Jackson Munro, Evanston’s Blake Peters and Niles Notre Dame’s Louis Lesmond all recently completed outstanding careers at Dartmouth, Princeton and Harvard, respectively. And current Ivy League players like Benet’s Niko Abusara at Dartmouth and Princeton’s tandem of Downers Grove North’s Jack Stanton and Young’s Dalen Davis continue to make their mark.</p><p>Bolte, who led St. Ignatius to 27 wins last season and is now a freshman at Yale, certainly noticed the local prep stars heading to the Ivy League and thriving once there.</p><p>“When it started to get real during my junior year, I did start to pay more attention to the Chicago area pipeline to the Ivy League,” Bolte said of his recent recruitment. “I started to want to be one of those names. I saw what John Poulakidas did when he went to Yale. And even Caden Pierce with what he did at Princeton and how he’s able to go to Purdue now. I definitely wanted to be in a pipeline like that with all that success and the degree too.”</p><p>While the local players have thrived on the court, it’s also what an Ivy League school brings after they’re done playing basketball that’s so enticing. Whether it’s elite social networking, the prestige that comes with the degree or higher starting salaries in the workforce, the opportunities that present themselves are endless.</p><p>“I really wanted to be in a spot where it’s not just a four-year decision but a 40-year decision for me with the degree,” Bolte said. “So I did get lucky with Yale and the perfect balance with basketball and beyond.”</p>

entries.title: Blackhawks lambasted by TNT panel during loss to Panthers
entries.summary: <p>FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. — Viewers of TNT's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>-Panthers TV broadcast Wednesday were serenaded with vicious criticism of the Hawks all night long.</p><p>"I don't see a lot of identity," unfiltered analyst Paul Bissonnette said during the first intermission. "I see a soft team. They don't check well. They don't forecheck well. They don't really do anything well."</p><p>The Hawks played slightly better during the second and third periods, but they didn't do nearly enough in an eventual 5-3 loss — their fourth in a row and their 12th in 16 games this season — to make Bissonnette eat his words.</p><p>Connor Bedard had two assists and was engaged physically throughout the game, working hard to win pucks and even throwing a few sizable hits. He said the Hawks have had conversations about battling harder since the atrocious Red Wings game last week.</p><p>But <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/04/blackhawks-coach-jeff-blashill-criticism-lineup-systems" >coach Jeff Blashill</a> felt that mantra still wasn't embraced equally by everyone Wednesday.</p><p>"[It's] not necessarily about the physicality, just the competition level to win battles," Blashill said. "[Bedard] competed like crazy. For not every guy to follow that suit is not acceptable. A lot of guys did, but you've got to have 20 going."</p><p>Frank Nazar snapped a seven-game goalless drought with two third-period tallies to cut what was once a 3-0 deficit to 4-3, but the Hawks weren't particularly dangerous offensively on the whole. They recorded only 20 total shots on goal.</p><h3><b>TNT’s view</b></h3><p>Bissonnette shredded the Hawks repeatedly, calling them "brutal" and unwatchable, while fellow panelist Henrik Lundqvist offered some less flamboyant yet wise commentary.</p><p>"When you're in a rebuild and you try and get out of it, to win consistently in this game, it's not about being the best team every night, but you have to be smart and you have to have awareness," Lundqvist said. </p><p>"You see sometimes the lack of awareness from young teams. When you watch Florida, they're not always the best team, but they're playing winning hockey. That will save you so many nights."</p><p>Blashill later said he disagreed with Bissonnette, but he accurately noted that "when you have the record that we have, you put yourself in position to be criticized."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Biz was very blunt about the Hawks:<br><br>"I see a soft team... they don't really do anything well" 😳<br><br>Then broke down their troubles with the help of the whiteboard <a href="https://t.co/IWasxvqECJ">pic.twitter.com/IWasxvqECJ</a></p>— NHLonTNT (@NHL_On_TNT) <a href="https://x.com/NHL_On_TNT/status/2118154646120206622?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 5, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Boucher’s debut</b></h3><p>The Hawks were without Patrick Kane, out with an upper-body injury, and they'll definitely be without him again Thursday against the Lightning. Blashill ruled him "doubtful" for Saturday at the Hurricanes, too.</p><p>Dillon Boucher replaced Kane in the lineup, making his NHL debut at 29 years old. Boucher is a nice story, having worked his way up through four years of Canadian college hockey, three years in the ECHL and one in the AHL.</p><p>Boucher is an enforcer whom Blashill called a "galvanizing guy," but he was unable to find any Panthers willing to fight during his eight minutes of ice time.</p>

entries.title: Bulls embarrassed in New York as rookie Caleb Wilson gets soft benching
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK – It feels a little different for Josh Giddey.</p><p>Like both he and the Bulls offense are taking steps towards progress. Baby steps, but steps.</p><p>All but meaningless on nights like Wednesday, however, when the defense was so non-existent from the opening tip-off that any gains by the offense were lost in the sewage displayed on the other end of the floor.</p><p>If there was some saving grace in an embarrassing 135-105 performance on the big stage of Madison Square Garden, it was at least the players didn’t wait until the third quarter to disappoint coach Tiago Splitter.</p><p>No, they handled that business right away as the defending NBA Champions got what ever they wanted in the opening stanza, jumping out to a 43-21 lead and doing so on 15-of-23 shooting (65.2%).</p><p>That also included the defense having no answer for Finals MVP Jalen Brunson, who put up 22 points in the first quarter alone. The Bulls (1-7) attempted to button things up in the second, but if only allowing 41 points on 59% shooting from the field is cleaning it up, heck, don’t bother.</p><p>All the Bulls did in that first half was allow the Knicks to tie a franchise record of 84 points scored going into the halftime locker room.</p><p>If there was some sort of light in a very dark tunnel, it was Giddey slowly finding his efficiency. Considering the hellish schedule the Bulls have been crawling through, he’ll need it.</p><p>“Yeah, I think so,” Giddey replied when asked if the team could come out of the gauntlet of games with enough calluses to start winning games. “I wouldn’t say there are any nights in the NBA where you’re like, ‘Ah, it’s a walkover.’ Especially a group like us where we feel like we can be competitive any night but we feel like we can also lose any night, so we got to come in with the right attitude, whether we’re playing the Knicks, who just won a championship, or a team that hasn’t won many games. We’ve got to respect our opponent.</p><p>“I think wins will start to come. We’re headed in the right direction, doing the right things and wins will start to come. Just stick with it.”</p><p>Advice he might want to remind himself of and his rookie Caleb Wilson.</p><p>It was an off night for the No. 4 pick, scoring just five points and not showcasing the best body language throughout the game. Enough so that after his third-quarter stint, Splitter sat him for the rest of the game.</p><p>“I didn’t think he had a great game,” Splitter said. “He wasn’t doing the right things on offense, defense, body language, he’s got to get better.”</p><p>The buzzword was resiliency, but not just for the 20-year-old. Giddey included. The veteran guard knows there is a lot more he needs to fix, but hitting three of his first four shots on his way to 10 points and six assists was something. Not enough, but something.</p><p>“I asked him to be aggressive, be yourself,” Splitter said of Giddey. “I think he tried to play the way we want.”</p><p>Now he needs to start playing the way he’s shown he can.</p><p>Giddey entered the rematch with the Knicks on Wednesday, averaging 9.1 points, 7.9 assists and 5.1 rebounds per game, shooting a dismal 26.9% from three-point range. Last season alone, Giddey was a 17-point scorer each game, as well as adding 9.1 rebounds and 8.3 rebounds per game, shooting 36.4% from three.</p><p>Splitter has been trying to stagger Giddey with the second unit, which has shown signs.</p><p>“I think I can be a lot more efficient, be stronger getting downhill, but overall, we’re taking steps in the right direction,” Giddey said. “It hasn’t shown in the win column, but I feel like we’re getting better and better.”</p><p>Now for that defense …</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Young trespassers were playing with fire
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> There is an 8-foot privacy fence all around my backyard, except for a small path that goes from the corner of the driveway around the side of the house. You can't see the path or the backyard from the street.</p><p>The other evening, I was grilling dinner when a pair of young women walked right up inside the fence. One of them introduced herself as a college student from Europe. At first, I thought they were hurt or something and needed help, but then they said they were selling magazines.</p><p>I asked them to back off my property and told them that strangers needed to use the front door to people's houses. I wanted to add that, at least where I live, it can be dangerous to trespass, and they were lucky my dog was inside.</p><p>It seems obvious to me that backyards, especially fenced ones, are private, and they should have known better. Then I got to wondering if that is true everywhere. Are there places where letting yourself into a stranger's fenced yard would be OK? (As an aside, I know they were probably not college students or legitimately selling magazines — that's an old one.) — <i>PRIVATE PROPERTY</i></p><p><b>DEAR PRIVATE PROPERTY:</b> You are correct on every level. What these young women did was foolish, rude, illegal and potentially dangerous. In Europe, just as in the U.S., a backyard is sacrosanct, and strangers should never enter without an invitation. These "students" were playing dumb because they got caught, and every part of their story is pure malarkey.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Fifty-two years ago, while in high school, I met a young lady. We hung out then and for two years after graduation. We did everything together, and at the time it seemed she was my soulmate. Then I dumped her with no explanation except that I had met someone else. I married that someone else within a year.</p><p>Twenty years went by, and during that time I reached out to the first lady a few times to wish her happy birthday and say that I hope all is well. After a few attempts at this, I received a certified letter saying I was to have no contact with her; otherwise, attorneys would become involved. It has now been 30 years of silence between us.</p><p>For more than half a century, I never thought about needing to apologize for leading that woman on when she was expecting our relationship to lead to marriage. In your opinion, would it be right to send her a letter to apologize for all the years of never saying I'm sorry, I was insensitive, and I was an idiot? — <i>ANOTHER DUMB MALE</i></p><p><b>DEAR MALE:</b> What part of "no contact" don't you understand? This woman wants nothing to do with you, and rightly so. You broke her heart. No matter how profusely and sincerely you apologize, she is not going to forgive you. The letter you want to send would be for your benefit, not hers. Stop being selfish, and let her leave that emotional trauma in the distant past.</p><p>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127. </p>

entries.title: Don't credit Trump with drop in crime
entries.summary: <p>Survey data published last week shows a <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/violent-crime-victimization-2025-survey-data/" target="_blank" >sharp decrease</a> in violent crime from 2024 to 2025, which is consistent with <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/08/15/trump-touts-new-stats-low-crime-crime-has-been-falling-years/" target="_blank" >FBI numbers</a> released last summer. Although the Trump administration has tried to <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/10/new-survey-president-trump-delivers-historic-drop-in-violent-crime/" target="_blank" >take credit</a> for that welcome development, there are several reasons to doubt such claims.</p><p>In August, the FBI <a class="Link" href="https://www.fbi.gov/news/press-releases/fbi-releases-2025-reported-crimes-in-the-nation-statistics" target="_blank" >reported</a> that the U.S. homicide rate fell by 18% from 2024 to 2025, an unprecedented drop. According to <a class="Link" href="https://counciloncj.org/crime-trends-in-u-s-cities-year-end-2025-update/" target="_blank" >data</a> compiled by the Council on Criminal Justice, the 2025 rate was the lowest recorded since at least 1900, and the rate is <a class="Link" href="https://counciloncj.org/homicide-likely-reaching-a-new-historic-low-as-most-crime-rates-continue-to-decline-at-mid-year/" target="_blank" >likely</a> to reach "a new historic low" this year.</p><p>"We have the numbers down because of what the federal government's doing," President Donald Trump <a class="Link" href="https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-speech-crime-statistics-prevention-enforcement-garden-city-new-york-august-14-2026/" target="_blank" >averred</a> during an Aug. 14 speech at the Nassau County, New York, police academy. "Everyone knows we've done an amazing job."</p><p>Four days later, a White House <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/08/president-trump-delivers-largest-drop-in-violent-crime-in-american-history/" target="_blank" >news release</a> reinforced that message. "President Trump Delivers the Largest Drop in Violent Crime in American History," the headline said.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-790000" name="module-790000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Trump "backed law enforcement, empowered the FBI to hunt predators instead of political targets, and rejected the failed Democrat lunacy that left communities reeling," the White House bragged. "The results are clear: fewer murders, fewer victims and safer streets."</p><p>That pattern repeated after the Justice Department <a class="Link" href="https://bjs.ojp.gov/document/pvencvs25.pdf" target="_blank" >announced</a> the preliminary results of the 2025 National Crime Victimization Survey last week. The 2025 <a class="Link" href="https://bjs.ojp.gov/document/pvencvs25.pdf" target="_blank" >victimization rate</a> for nonfatal violent crime, excluding simple assault, was 7.4 per 1,000 Americans 12 or older, down 25% from 2024.</p><p>"President Trump Delivers Historic Drop in Violent Crime," the White House <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/10/new-survey-president-trump-delivers-historic-drop-in-violent-crime/" target="_blank" >crowed</a>. "Violent crime PLUMMETED in 2025 compared to 2024," Attorney General Todd Blanche <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/AGToddBlanche/status/2114710803882360962" target="_blank" >said</a>. "This is what happens when you have an administration [that] prioritizes the safety and security of Americans and our communities."</p><p>Inconveniently for Trump, the downward trend in violent crime <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/08/15/trump-touts-new-stats-low-crime-crime-has-been-falling-years/" target="_blank" >began</a> in 2023, two years before he started his current term. And if Trump deserves credit for the continuation of that trend, doesn't he also deserve blame for the <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/reoord-spike-murders-2020/2020/12/30/1dcb057c-4ae5-11eb-839a-cf4ba7b7c48c_story.html" target="_blank" >huge 2020 spike</a> in homicides, which likewise happened on his watch?</p><p>The truth is that neither inference is justified without additional evidence. Presidents have a limited role in law enforcement, which is primarily a state and local function, and many factors other than federal policy affect crime rates.</p><p>In September, the Council on Criminal Justice <a class="Link" href="https://counciloncj.org/executive-summary-whats-driving-the-homicide-decline/" target="_blank" >convened</a> a panel of 48 crime experts to assess four dozen possible explanations for the recent decline in homicides. <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/10/07/a-survey-of-crime-experts-deflates-the-trump-effect-that-supposedly-reduced-homicides/" target="_blank" >None of them</a> thought the federal policies highlighted by Trump had played a major role.</p><p>Not a single expert said Trump's National Guard deployments had made a "major" contribution, and just one perceived a "limited" impact. No one listed that factor as a top-five contributor. Nor did anyone mention increased immigration enforcement as a top contributor, although two participants said it had played a "limited" role.</p><p>The Council on Criminal Justice did not specifically ask about FBI arrests, another explanation favored by Trump. The survey did ask about improvements in homicide clearance rates, which 11% of the experts viewed as a top contributor. But since the FBI accounts for a small share of <a class="Link" href="https://www.fbi.gov/news/stories/violent-crime-falls-at-historic-rate-new-fbi-data-show" target="_blank" >violent crime arrests</a> (about <a class="Link" href="https://www.fbi.gov/news/speeches-and-testimony/a-review-of-the-president-s-fiscal-year-2027-budget-request-for-the-fbi-the-dea-the-usms-and-the-atf" target="_blank" >8% </a>in 2025), Trump is surely overrating the agency's role in reducing homicides.</p><p>Less concretely, the experts weighed the potential impact of "presidential public safety signals." Three participants credited that factor with a "limited" impact, and none thought it was a top contributor.</p><p>The most strongly favored explanation was "easing pandemic-related social and economic disruption," which 57% of the experts deemed "a major contributor." Other factors with relatively high scores included expansion of community violence prevention programs, increased use of "focused deterrence" aimed at "high-risk individuals and groups," increases in local government capacity, and increases in public safety and support services "relative to demand."</p><p>These assessments are a work in progress, and firmer answers won't be possible without further research. But one thing seems clear: Trump's policies fall woefully short of explaining recent declines in violent crime.</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b50000" name="module-b50000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: Trump tumbles hard
entries.summary: <p>For many Americans, the last decade of politics has tested their patience — and the laws of physics.</p><p>Donald Trump’s rise from reality star to president has been marked by jaw-dropping moments that seemed to bend the conventions long held not only by conservatives and Republicans, but by the world as we know it.</p><p>His unseemly personal peccadillos didn’t hurt him. His ugly attacks on people usually spared by smart politicians — and decent people — like veterans, disabled people, women and children didn’t turn off a majority of voters. His open grifting and profiteering off of his own impeachments and mugshot didn’t keep him from reelection — nor did those criminal convictions.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a20000" name="module-a20000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Nor did instigating an insurrection at the U.S. Capitol, in which his supporters attacked police officers and American democracy itself.</p><p>But last night, the laws of physics proved immutable, to the relief of millions of Americans.</p><p>Gravity is, in fact, real.</p><p>It turns out, you can’t <a class="Link" href="https://www.livenowfox.com/news/trump-admits-war-iran-contributed-midterm-election-results" target="_blank" >start a war in the Middle East in an election year</a> after promising you wouldn’t.</p><p>It turns out, you can’t raise gas prices as a result of that unpopular war and then tell people to suck it up — it’s patriotic.</p><p>It turns out you can’t raise the cost of goods on everything from groceries to energy with tariffs — a tax on consumers — <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2025/12/11/nx-s1-5639957/trump-affordability-hoax-economy-midterms" target="_blank" >and then tell people affordability is “a hoax.”</a> Again, in an election year.</p><p>It turns out you can’t openly use the presidency to line your own pockets and the pockets of your family; you can’t party with caviar bars and live zebras and brag about how much the oil companies are making off the ill-advised war no one voted for while most Americans are struggling to feed their families.</p><p>It turns out you can’t break a bunch of core promises to voters — to end inflation, to end forever wars, to release the Epstein files, to name just a few — and expect them to take it on the chin.</p><p>It turns out unelected tech bros can’t just buy elections, even with nearly half a billion dollars.</p><p>And it turns out, you can’t ask voters to <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/04/us/video/trump-approval-rating-midterms-harry-enten-intldsk" target="_blank" >pretend you’re on the ballot with just 30% approval</a>.</p><p>On Tuesday night, voters all over the map, including in the reddest of states and counties, sent a message to Trump and the Republicans who enabled him that they were done with the nonsense, the self-dealing, the broken promises, the open corruption, the let-them-eat-cake largesse and the focus on everything but the things that matter to them.</p><p>To say Democrats overperformed is an understatement. With wins everywhere from Texas to South Carolina, Dems took back the House and the Senate with seats to spare and won a majority of governors races. It’s harder to find the places where Republicans actually had some wins — and can they really brag about winning in Florida, the president’s home state?</p><p>Sen.-elect James Talarico won in Texas by a whopping 12 points.</p><p>Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton won by four points in Kansas.</p><p>Sen.-elect Troy Jackson won by eight points in Maine.</p><p>Sen.-elect Annie Andrews won in South Carolina by three points.</p><p>The question now is, will Trump and MAGA learn the very clear lesson voters taught them? Will Republican lawmakers begin to pry Trump’s bloated fingers off their party as the sun sets on his second term? Will they reject Trump’s culture wars and return to the principles that drew Americans to the right in the first place?</p><p>Trump seemed to believe “total immunity” wasn’t just a legal application but a political one. It turns out, it wasn’t. Not even he was immune from his own bad decisions and the will of the people.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a80000" name="module-a80000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: Landmark status sought for Lake View house tied to city's early preservation movement
entries.summary: <p>An architect's 19th century Lake View graystone — home base for his successful efforts to preserve Louis Sullivan's architecture and legacy — is being considered for preliminary landmark status.</p><p>The Commission on Chicago Landmarks will decide Thursday whether to designate the residence and studio of long-time architect and preservationist John Vinci.</p><p>In addition to the two-flat building's architecture, the designation would also honor Vinci's groundbreaking preservation work and his architectural firm that was founded in the two-story home's dining room in 1969.</p><p>Vinci could become the second Chicago architect to have his house landmarked while he's still residing there. A city spokesperson said the first was likely William Keck, who was 85 and living in the modernist Keck-Gottschalk-Keck Apartments, 5551 S. University Ave., when the building he designed with his brother, George, was designated in 1994.</p><p>"To be honest I'm sort of embarrassed," Vinci, 89, said of his home's designation. "But I think the house is worth it."</p><p>Built in 1893, the home at 3152 N. Cambridge Ave. is no doubt a looker with its corner tower and arched first-floor windows.</p><p>Vinci replaced the house's concrete porch and front steps with a steel one made from his own design. The 2009 addition is a light, almost transparent, touch that doesn't distract from the building's classic Indiana limestone facade.</p><p>And there's an added treat for those who find themselves in the alley along the south side of the house: a two-story bay window with curved glass. </p><p>Graceful and trimmed in metal, the restored window is a detail as Victorian as Ulster coats and opera LaSalle St., and the reconstruction of the space at the Art Institute of Chicago. </p><p>Another habitue was Vinci's friend and college classmate Richard Nickel, a prominent founder of the Chicago preservation movement, who was killed in 1972 while salvaging architectural materials from the building as it was under demolition.</p><p>"This was his last stop," Vinci said of his home. And the building collapsed on him."</p><p>"Nickel, obviously, is really important," Cahan, a Nickel biographer, said. "He did start the preservation movement in Chicago. But John is important because he took that start and ran with it."</p>

"We were like two outlaws," says Binion. “He was doing his own thing.”</p><h3><b>Deep personal explorations of anxiety </b></h3><p>Johnson’s first photo series, “Seeing in the Dark,” shows that unconventional spirit. entries.title: How Bob Newhart, one-time failed Chicago accountant, became one of America’s most-loved comedians
entries.summary: <p>Bob Newhart’s face did not age well.</p><p>But in the deepening lines, hollowing cheeks and weary eyes, audiences were reminded of what had always made his comedy so irresistible, so universal: a look that said, “I can’t believe I’m having to deal with this crap.”</p><p>That silent comedy is a big part of why the Oak Park-born, Cubs-loving, failed accountant endured as one of America’s most-loved comedians for more than six decades.</p><p>Newhart’s life in comedy is now meticulously chronicled in “Bob Newhart: The Life and Laughter of an American Treasure” ($28, Citadel; out Oct. 23).</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-6a0000" name="image-6a0000"></a> </div> </div><p>“That was the genius of Bob Newhart, who managed to stay ‘in vogue’ throughout his long career … because he appealed to so many different segments of society without ever altering the ingredients that were mixed into his recipe for success — that magical mélange of humility, gentle humor, and grace that endeared him to his admirers,” writes the book’s author, Michael Seth Starr, a former New York Post reporter and columnist who has penned biographies of numerous celebrities, including Ringo Starr, William Shatner and Rodney Dangerfield.</p><p>Pull up the classic Newhart stage monologue online, and the imagined phone conversation between a PR man <a class="Link" href="https://www.c-span.org/clip/national-press-club/user-clip-bob-newhart-does-his-lincoln-phone-gag-at-npc-1995/4526484" target="_blank" >begging the president</a> not to tweak his soon-to-be-delivered Gettysburg Address (“You changed four score and seven to eighty-seven?”) feels as fresh and hilarious as the day it was written.</p><p>The same can be said of Professor Proton in <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WbhiNN_NaEk" target="_blank" ><u>“The Big Bang Theory,”</u></a> or as Dr. Robert Hartley, a Chicago-based psychologist in <a class="Link" href="https://www.imdb.com/video/embed/vi468299545/" target="_blank" ><u>“The Bob Newhart Show.”</u></a> In all of those, he’s essentially the same stuttering, twitchy and often befuddled everyman character — and one that never got old.</p><p>Newhart was born in Oak Park and grew up on the West Side, went to St. Ignatius High School (now College Prep) and earned a bachelor’s degree in management (with an emphasis in accounting) from Loyola University Chicago. While in college, he dabbled in theater and wrote humorous sketches.</p><p>Newhart had Chicago to thank for a series of dreary jobs — in accounting and behind the counter at the Illinois State Compensation Board — that would later help him connect with everyday people and feel their pain.</p><p>And, Starr writes, he got a big boost from Chicago DJ Dan Sorkin who, in the late 1950s, saw something fresh and very funny in a young Newhart.</p><p>“He came along at a time when he wasn’t telling the mother-in-law jokes. He wasn’t a stand-up comedian per se, like Rodney Dangerfield or Don Rickles, who could fire off [jokes] rat-a-tat-tat. He told stories or he told interactions, and these had never been heard before in the comedy world,” Starr said during a recent chat with the Sun-Times.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-760001" name="image-760001"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/41019dc/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2308x1295+0+891/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F14%2Fe1%2Ffbe886bb46aba94f5ddf465b7f29%2Fstarr-michael-seth-2026-photo-credit-gail-starr.jpeg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/94809bb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2308x1295+0+891/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F14%2Fe1%2Ffbe886bb46aba94f5ddf465b7f29%2Fstarr-michael-seth-2026-photo-credit-gail-starr.jpeg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e0fbac3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2308x1295+0+891/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F14%2Fe1%2Ffbe886bb46aba94f5ddf465b7f29%2Fstarr-michael-seth-2026-photo-credit-gail-starr.jpeg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Starr, Michael Seth 2026 - Newhart’s first comedy album, “The Button-Down Mind of Bob Newhart,” shot to the top of the Billboard charts, as did the comedian’s follow-up album. By the end of 1961, he was in demand, doing nightclub shows across the United States and appearing frequently on national TV, including “The Ed Sullivan Show” and “The Tonight Show Starring Jack
